experiment_plans.feasibility_notes: The hypothesis is feasible given the compute and data constraints. The required dataset 'fama_french_three_factor_daily_returns.csv' is available and contains the necessary macroeconomic factors (Mkt-RF, SMB, HML). The experiment can be conducted using a standard multi-task learning setup with a single GPU node for a few hours. The credit risk dataset 'uci_statlog_german_credit.csv' is also available and suitable for borrower-level feature modeling. The experiment will train a multi-task model with auxiliary targets and compare it to a single-task model, both on the same credit risk data.
experiment_plans.objective: To determine whether incorporating Fama-French three-factor returns (Mkt-RF, SMB, HML) as auxiliary prediction targets in a multi-task learning model for credit default prediction improves out-of-sample AUC performance compared to a single-task model trained only on borrower-level features.
experiment_plans.design: A comparative benchmark experiment where we train two models: a single-task model that predicts credit default solely from borrower-level features, and a multi-task model that additionally predicts the Fama-French factors as auxiliary tasks. We will compare their out-of-sample AUC performance on a held-out test set.

data_requirements.description: This dataset contains 1000 German credit records with 20 borrower-level features and a binary credit risk outcome (good/bad). It is suitable for credit default prediction and provides the necessary borrower-level features for our models.
preprocessing_steps: Load the dataset and remove the target variable 'credit_risk' from features
Encode categorical variables using one-hot encoding
Normalize numerical features to zero mean and unit variance
Merge with Fama-French factors from 'fama_french_three_factor_daily_returns.csv' using date matching
Create time-lagged features for borrower data to align with macroeconomic periods

methods.name: Multi-task deep learning
methods.description: A neural network architecture with shared layers followed by task-specific heads for credit default prediction and the three Fama-French factors. The shared representation learns common patterns between tasks while task-specific layers adapt to each prediction goal.

methods.name: Deep Neural Networks (DNN)
methods.description: A feedforward neural network with hidden layers to learn non-linear relationships between borrower features and credit risk, as well as between macroeconomic factors and credit risk.

evaluation.baseline: Single-task model trained only on borrower-level features without auxiliary macroeconomic targets
evaluation.success_criteria: If the multi-task model achieves higher AUC than the single-task model on out-of-sample test data, the hypothesis is supported. If the AUC is equal or lower, the hypothesis is refuted.

implementation_steps.description: Load and preprocess the uci_statlog_german_credit.csv dataset, including categorical encoding and normalization of numerical features
Load and preprocess the fama_french_three_factor_daily_returns.csv dataset, converting date formats and ensuring proper alignment with credit data
Merge the credit data with macroeconomic factors using date matching to create aligned time-series features
Create a multi-task DNN model with shared layers for borrower features and separate heads for credit default prediction and Fama-French factor prediction
Train the multi-task model on the training set with appropriate loss weighting for both tasks
Train a single-task DNN model on the same borrower features but only for credit default prediction
Evaluate both models on the test set using AUC as the primary metric
Compare AUC scores between the multi-task and single-task models to determine if auxiliary factors improve performance

risks: Insufficient temporal alignment between borrower data and macroeconomic factors
Overfitting due to limited sample size (1000 observations) in the credit dataset
Negative transfer between tasks if the auxiliary factors don't provide useful signal for credit prediction
Computational cost exceeding SLURM allocation limits if model complexity is too high
